abstract: Inborn errors of immunity (IEIs), such as Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD), impose a disproportionately severe clinical burden in populations with high rates of consanguinity. CGD is caused by defects in the phagocyte NADPH oxidase complex, frequently due to mutations in the NCF1 gene encoding the p47phox protein. While the functional domains of NCF1 are well characterized, the quantitative architectural constraints governing its structural stability remain elusive. This study aimed to decipher the multidimensional quantitative signatures of NCF1, across diverse organisms in order to understand its conserved spatial sequence architecture and the structural basis of variant severity. We analyzed 41 NCF1 sequences using ten distinct quantitative features, integrating primary sequence metrics, biophysical chemistry, and abstract topological geometry. The synthesis of these features revealed a lack of a unified proximity matrix, demonstrating that NCF1 is defined by feature-dependent, multidimensional individual signatures. Primary sequence metrics exhibited rigid phylogenetic conservation, revealing invariant zero-entropy blocks that correlated strictly with severe CGD-causing mutations, while topological metrics exposed a deep spatial architectural convergence. These multidimensional baselines confirmed that the protein requires a highly specific spatial packing to assemble the NADPH oxidase complex; pathogenic mutations therefore disrupt precise structural signatures rather than globally destroying the protein. Consistent with this, the AlphaFold model places the folded PX and tandem SH3 domains in a high-confidence core and the regulatory C-terminal tail in an exposed, low-confidence region, supporting a tail-mediated autoinhibitory mechanism. Ultimately, this quantitative framework offers a useful perspective on NCF1 architecture and may serve as a supportive tool for evaluating the severity of clinical variants, contributing to precision medicine efforts for NCF1-associated diseases.
